title: Well and House
premise: Folklorist Hazel Iversen arrives in the drowned valley village of Marrow's Rest to record its songs, only to find every ballad ends mid-verse, as if cut off. When a church bell that was melted down in 1911 begins ringing at dawn, she learns the founders bound something beneath the well to protect the village—a bargain renewed each generation by a keeper who must belong completely. The last keeper died without an heir, and the songs are the ritual fraying. Hazel, an outsider who has spent her life observing rather than belonging, discovers her own bloodline ties her to the founders' covenant. To save the village she must finish the interrupted ritual—singing the final verse inside the well itself—which demands she surrender her records, her name, and her selfhood to become the new keeper, choosing love for a place that never truly wanted her over the survival of her own identity.
about_author: Lior Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing oral histories in remote coastal communities before turning to fiction. They write horror about the violence hidden in tradition and the terrible intimacy of small places.

chapters.title: The Songs That End Mid-Verse
chapters.summary: Hazel arrives in Marrow's Rest with recording equipment and scholarly detachment, welcomed with polite warmth that stops short of invitation. An old woman, Edith Crane, sings a harvest ballad that breaks off abruptly; when Hazel asks for the ending, Edith goes pale and refuses. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: curiosity sharpening into unease—the first crack in her belief that observation is harmless.

chapters.title: A Bell With No Bell
chapters.summary: At dawn Hazel is woken by bell-ringing, but the parish records confirm the church bell was melted for scrap in 1911. Villagers deny hearing anything; the vicar's hands shake as he pours her tea. She finds wax drippings on the empty belfry beam. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: isolation deepens—she realizes the village shares a silence she isn't part of.

chapters.title: What the Well Keeps
chapters.summary: Following the songs' shared imagery, Hazel locates the old well behind the ruined founder's house. Peering in, she hears a chorus humming below—her own recordings, played back wrong. A boy, Tam, warns her: 'It learns you if you listen back.' POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: dread replacing academic thrill; the archive has become an audience.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession
chapters.summary: Edith reveals the covenant: the founders drowned their own song in the well to buy the village safety from the famine years, and each generation a keeper renews it by singing the verse they refused to finish. The last keeper, Maren, died childless two winters ago. Edith begs Hazel to leave before the thing below finishes learning her voice. POV: alternating Hazel and Edith. Emotional beat: grief and guilt—the village's kindness was always fear.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Blood
chapters.summary: Researching Maren's papers, Hazel finds genealogies proving she descends from one of the founders who fled before the ritual was completed—hers is the blood meant to close the circle. Her presence wasn't accident; the well called her. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: betrayal by her own history; belonging revealed as inheritance she never chose.

chapters.title: Tam's Verse
chapters.summary: The boy Tam, secretly Maren's grandson, has been singing fragments to the well out of loneliness—and it has begun answering him in his dead grandmother's voice. Hazel realizes the entity will take him if no keeper acts. She starts teaching him protection charms while hiding her plan. POV: Tam, then Hazel. Emotional beat: fierce tenderness; love against duty takes shape.

chapters.title: The Night of Rising Water
chapters.summary: The well floods the low fields; the dead founders' voices walk the lanes singing the missing verse in Hazel's mother's intonation. The village finally admits what it has denied, turning to her not with welcome but demand. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: fury and clarity—they want a sacrifice, not a savior, and she sees it plainly.

chapters.title: Everything Documented Is Everything Lost
chapters.summary: Hazel understands the ritual's price: the keeper must give the well her records—every song, every name, every proof she existed—so the entity can wear a complete life instead of taking living ones. She spends her last night transcribing nothing, burning nothing, simply listening to her tapes one final time. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: mourning herself in advance; documentation as prayer becomes farewell.

chapters.title: The Final Verse
chapters.summary: At dawn Hazel descends into the well singing the interrupted ballad, Tam holding the rope, the whole village gathered in silence. Below, the founders' chorus rises to meet her, and she gives them her archives, her name, her voice—finishing the verse as the water closes. The bell rings once, whole and real, then stops forever. POV: Tam. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into awe; witness as the only inheritance left.

chapters.title: The Song Sung Twice
chapters.summary: A year later, Tam tends the well and teaches the children the complete ballad—the first time in a century it can be sung twice. Edith leaves flowers at the belfry. In the village school, a new folklorist arrives asking questions, and Tam feels the well hum softly, patient, content—for now. POV: Tam. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; belonging purchased at a price the village will never fully understand.
